<reason>CON's opening move — anchoring the debate on the existing "undue hardship" standard and reframing PRO's ask as ripping the door off its hinges rather than opening one — set up a durable structural advantage. The decisive exchange came when PRO, under pressure, specified a concrete mechanism (a time-and-income presumption with the burden flipped to lenders) while still claiming the filing-cost pain preserves deterrence. CON exploited this cleanly: a lender with no visibility into future earnings cannot meaningfully rebut a presumption, so the "filter" PRO claims to keep is exactly what PRO's own test deletes. PRO's closing reasserted that this was "adjudication, not abolition" without explaining how rebuttal would function in practice, leaving CON's contradiction unresolved. PRO's moral framing (the aide, the gambler comparison, the collateral-morality flip) was compelling and kept real pressure on CON to justify keeping any hardship-style bar, and CON never fully proved that streamlined proof alone would rescue the aide from garnishment on the timeline PRO describes. But on the central mechanical question — how do you make discharge "much easier" while preserving the deterrent PRO's own case depends on — CON forced PRO into an unresolved tension and hammered it home more precisely in both rebuttals and the closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B4.2]-[B4.4], catching PRO's own presumption/burden-flip proposal in the contradiction between "much easier" and "deterrent survives because filing itself is painful," crystallized in the closing line that PRO's fix is "discharge on a timer, dressed in adjudication's clothes."</best_rebuttal>
